tip: ‘ers’ marks how long something has held true: ‘ers ugain mlynedd’ = for twenty years. It normally pairs with the present tense.
‘Was born’ is ‘cafodd’ plus a possessive plus ‘geni’, literally ‘got their birth’: ‘cafodd hi ei geni’ = she was born.
Feminine ‘ei’ (her) is often echoed by ‘hi’ after the noun: ‘ei llais hi’ = her voice, which removes any his or her ambiguity.
Negative past of ‘bod’ uses ‘doedd’ with ‘ddim’: ‘doedd hi ddim’ = she was not.
‘ei’ meaning her aspirate-mutates p, t, c: ‘tad-cu’ becomes ‘thad-cu’, so ‘ei thad-cu’ = her grandfather.
‘roedd’ is the was/were form of ‘bod’ for he, she or it: ‘roedd deg cwestiwn’ = there were ten questions.
Twenty has its own word, ‘ugain’, a leftover of the old base-twenty counting system: ‘ugain tŷ’ = twenty houses.
‘bydda i’ is I will: ‘bydda i’n ymarfer’ = I will practise. Keep ‘yn’ before the verb, as in the present.
‘ei’ has two meanings: ‘ei’ (his) softens the next word, ‘ei’ (her) aspirates it. Here ‘ei phlant’ (her children) shows p to ph.
For writing or sending to a person, Welsh normally uses ‘at’, not ‘i’: ‘llythyr at ei mam-gu’ = a letter to her grandmother.
Masculine ‘ei’ (his) soft-mutates the next word: ‘teulu’ (family) becomes ‘ei deulu’ = his family.
Feminine ‘ei’ (her, its) aspirate-mutates p, t, c: ‘pobi’ becomes ‘phobi’ in ‘ei phobi’ = was baked.
Starting with a time word like ‘ddoe’ doesn't change the verb: ‘prynais i’ still carries the ‘-ais’ ending for I bought.
‘I was born’ is literally ‘I got my birth’: ‘cefais i fy ngeni’, using ‘cael’ plus ‘fy’ plus the verb.
‘yn’ (in) becomes ‘ym’ before m: ‘ym mis Medi’ = in September.
Welsh has no verb ‘to have’. Use ‘gyda’ (with): ‘does dim amser gyda ni’ = we have no time, literally no time with us.
‘mor’ before an adjective, plus ‘â’ (or ‘ag’ before a vowel), means as...as: ‘mor boeth ag’ = as hot as.
‘a’ marks a relative clause meaning who or which: ‘y ferch a enillodd y fedal’ = the girl who won the medal.
‘pe bai’ means if...were, for unreal or hypothetical situations: ‘pe bai'r trên ar amser’ = if the train were on time.
‘a’ (and) aspirate-mutates only the next word if it starts p, t or c: ‘caws’ becomes ‘chaws’, so ‘bara a chaws’ = bread and cheese.
‘gweld eisiau’ means to miss someone, literally to see a want: ‘roedd e'n gweld eisiau’ = he missed.
‘nid yn unig’ sets up not only, and pairs with ‘ond...hefyd’ (but also) later in the sentence.
Two has separate genders: ‘dau gi’ = two dogs, but ‘dwy gath’ = two cats. Both soft-mutate the noun after them.
‘rhaid i’ plus a subject means must: ‘rhaid i'r traethawd fod’ = the dissertation must be. Welsh frames obligation as necessity.
‘fy’ (my) nasal-mutates the next word, turning g into ng: ‘gwaith’ becomes ‘ngwaith’ in ‘fy ngwaith’.
‘o’ (of) soft-mutates the noun after it: ‘cadeiriau’ becomes ‘gadeiriau’, so ‘digon o gadeiriau’ = enough chairs.
‘a’ (and) aspirate-mutates a following p, t or c: ‘pob’ becomes ‘phob’ here in ‘a phob bendith’.
‘i'w’ is ‘i’ plus ‘ei’ (to its) and soft-mutates the verb: ‘gwastraffu’ becomes ‘wastraffu’ in ‘i'w wastraffu’ = to waste it.
The ‘-wch’ ending marks a plural or polite command: ‘arhoswch’ = wait, said to more than one person or formally.
‘dod’ (to come) is irregular in the past: ‘daeth’ = came, not a regular ending. ‘daeth ei rhieni’ = her parents came.
